steps.body: Four solving methods, one decision: bare x² = k or a ready-made square → **square roots**; friendly integer factors → **factoring**; even middle term, stubborn factors → **completing the square**; anything at all → the **formula**. The discriminant predicts the root type before you commit.

widget.prompt: Drag each equation to the method that solves it fastest.

items.label: x² − 16 = 0
items.feedback: Isolate and root: x = ±4 — no other machinery needed.

items.label: x² + 5x + 6 = 0
items.feedback: 2 and 3 multiply to 6 and add to 5: (x + 2)(x + 3) in one step.

items.label: x² + 6x − 1 = 0
items.feedback: b = 6 is even and −1 kills integer factoring — (x + 3)² = 10 is smooth.

items.label: 3x² − 2x + 7 = 0
items.feedback: a ≠ 1, nothing factors, odd middle — the formula grinds it out reliably.

widget.missFeedback: Match the equation's shape: bare square, friendly factors, even b, or none of the above.
widget.successFeedback: All four matched — the shape of the equation picks the tool.

steps.body: Complex roots aren't tied to any one method — they appear whenever **D < 0**, whichever route you take. x² + 10x + 29: completing the square gives (x + 5)² = −4, so x = **−5 ± 2i** — the negative square announces the complex pair.

explanationVariants: (x + 5)² = −4 gives x = −5 ± 2i; the root with positive imaginary part is −5 + 2i, imaginary part 2.
√(−4) = 2i sets the spread; the imaginary part is its coefficient, 2.

widget.prompt: Solve x² + 10x + 29 = 0 (hint: complete the square). For the root with POSITIVE imaginary part, what is the imaginary part?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the value of −k in (x + 5)² = −4 — take its square root: the spread is 2i, so the part is 2.
−5 is the REAL part (the center) — the imaginary part is the 2 from ±2i.

widget.prompt: Solve x² − 2x − 15 = 0 by the quickest route.

options.label: x = 5 or x = −3
options.feedback: Right — (x − 5)(x + 3): the numbers −5 and +3 multiply to −15 and add to −2. ✓

options.label: x = −5 or x = 3
options.feedback: Signs flipped: the factors are (x − 5)(x + 3), so the roots are +5 and −3.

options.label: x = 1 ± 4i
options.feedback: D = 4 + 60 = 64 > 0 — the roots are REAL here (5 and −3).

options.label: x = 5 or x = 3
options.feedback: The product of the roots must be c = −15, a NEGATIVE — one root of each sign: 5 and −3.

explanationVariants: x − 3 = ±7, so x = 10 or x = −4; the larger is 10.
The square is already isolated — root, then shift: 3 ± 7.

widget.prompt: Solve (x − 3)² = 49. What is the LARGER solution?

commonErrors.feedback: −4 is the smaller root (3 − 7) — the larger is 3 + 7 = 10.
The 3 shifts AFTER rooting: x = 3 ± 7, never 49 + 3.

explanationVariants: The formula needs no special shape — it solves every quadratic, real or complex roots alike.
Factoring and square-rooting need cooperation from the equation; the formula never does.

widget.prompt: Which method is guaranteed to solve ANY quadratic equation?

options.label: the quadratic formula
options.feedback: Right — it handles every a, b, c, and every discriminant sign.

options.label: factoring
options.feedback: Factoring needs integer-friendly roots — x² + 6x − 1 defeats it, but not the formula.

options.label: square roots
options.feedback: That needs the square pre-packaged (no loose x term) — most quadratics aren't.

options.label: reading the graph
options.feedback: Graphs can't show complex roots at all — the parabola never touches the axis when D < 0.

explanationVariants: Any method lands the same place: the conjugate pair 1 ± 2i.

options.label: x = 1 ± 2i
options.feedback: Right — divide by 2, then D = −16 gives (2 ± 4i)/2 = 1 ± 2i.

options.label: x = 2 ± 4i
options.feedback: Those are the formula's raw parts BEFORE dividing by 2a — halve both: 1 ± 2i.

options.label: x = −1 ± 2i
options.feedback: −b = +2 after dividing by 2 (or +4 before), so the real part is +1.

options.label: x = 1 ± 4i
options.feedback: The 4i still owes the ÷2: the spread is ±2i.

steps.body: Pick the method by the equation's shape — the answers don't care which you choose.
takeaways: Bare square → roots; friendly factors → factor; even b → complete; always → formula.
D < 0 predicts a conjugate pair before any solving starts.
Dividing by a first often simplifies everything.
steps.teaser: That completes Algebra 2's complex-number toolkit — polynomials of every degree are next.

concept.body: Shape picks the method. x² = 81 has no x term and no factoring puzzle — the square is already alone.

explanationVariants: With the square isolated, rooting both sides is one step.

widget.prompt: What is the fastest method for x² = 81?

options.label: the quadratic formula
options.feedback: It works, but it's the slow lane here — the square is already isolated: root it.

options.label: factoring
options.feedback: You could rewrite as a difference of squares, but rooting both sides is faster.

options.label: completing the square
options.feedback: The square is ALREADY complete — just take roots.
